newsitem.title: USA: Con Edison set to detail settlement.
newsitem.headline: Con Edison set to detail settlement.

text.p: Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc expects to release details of its settlement agreement with the New York Public Service Commission between 1000 and 1100 EST/1500 and 1600 GMT, spokesman Richard Mulleri said Thursday.
The latest deadline for the company's filing of a settlement with the commission is Thursday and commission spokesman David Flanagan said the utility is expected to do meet that deadline.
The settlement is the second stage in Con Edison's response to the commission's Competitive Opportunities Order.
Con Edison's original filing deadline under the order dated May 20, 1996, was October 1.

That filing led to talks with the commission staff about changes in the utility's proposal that were originally due to be filed with the commission on February 14. That deadline was extended several times.
There are not expected to be many surprises in Thursday's filing, as details have leaked out over the past two weeks.
Intervenors in the commission proceeding that led to May's order say about 80 participants in those talks received "confidential" updates on the talks.
Twenty of those intervenors wrote New York Governor George Pataki Tuesday saying they had been shut out of the talks.

"Now that the commission's goals are being translated into concrete action plans, we are being shut out of the process. Secret negotiations ... are producing written agreements which do not address the concerns of a majority of New York's constituents. Previous visionary statements from your commission are being replaced with timid proposals that promise only minor rate reductions ... and a virtual moratorium on competition," they wrote.
In its original filing, Con Edison had proposed a rate freeze during the transition to competition.

The complaining intervenors noted reports the company had agreed to indjustrial rate reductions that exceed those given to residential and commercial customers by seven to one and two to one, respectively, while delaying customer choice for a vast majority of customers until after the year 2000.
Con Edison's financial condition is such that the company apparently decided it was better to negotiate immediate rate cuts than to allow real competition, one intervenor said.
"If you're first you can call the shots to some extent" appears to be the utility's bargaining stance, he added.
Paul C. Rapp said there's "not enough of a break" in the published proposals for anyone.
Rapp, a lawyer with Cohen, Dax & Koenig, has the Retail Council of New York and one retailer, May Department Stores Co, among his clients.
He is concerned the "institutionalized changes (being discussed) are not great enough to encourage competition."
Enron Corp is "very concerned that the strong vision the commission laid out" in May "will not come to fruition," Howard Former said.
The company is very anxious to come into the New York market, he pointed out.
Originally, he said, this was a restructuring case. Rates were almost an afterthought.
"We've turned this into a rate case and forgotten the restructuring," Former said.
